parole.testo: From Middle High German vloite and variants; borrowed via Middle Dutch floite from Old French fleüte.
From (late) Middle High German franze, which is borrowed via Middle Dutch from Old French frenge.
Diminutive of an obsolete simplex frett, which is borrowed via Middle Dutch furet, fret from Old French furet, + -chen. Compare modern Dutch fret.
From late Middle Dutch jueel and its modern continuation in Dutch juweel. The Dutch word is borrowed from Old French jouel.

parole.significato: to nought, to nullify, to quash, to cassate
parole.testo: From Middle High German kassieren (West Central German, 14th c.), probably from Middle Dutch casseren (13th c.), from Old French casser, quasser (“to annul”). Ultimately from a merger of Latin cassāre and quassāre. The German may later have been reinforced also by Italian cassare, from the same Lati

From Middle High German kástel (“fortified castle, city”), from Old High German kastel, and its doublet Middle High German kastḗl (“castle”), from Middle Dutch casteel, from Picardian Old French castel. Both ultimately from Latin castellum, which also directly influenced the modern form and sense.

parole.significato: a case; a suitcase or briefcase
parole.testo: From Late Middle High German koffer, from Middle Dutch coffer, from Old French cofre.
From Middle Dutch net (“neat, decent, pretty”), from Old French net (“neat, decent”), from Latin nitidus. Compare English neat.

parole.significato: park (piece of ground in or near a city or town, enclosed and kept for ornament and recreation)
parole.testo: A doublet of inherited Pferch (“pen [for animals]”). The form Park was first borrowed in the 15th/16th centuries from Middle Dutch park, in which the word had developed the sense “recreation park, enclosed hunting grounds” under the influence of Old French parc. German Park remained sporadic, howeve

Inherited from Middle High German pastēde, likely from Middle Dutch pasteide, from Old French pasté, from Late Latin pasta (“paste, dough, pastry cake”). See there for more. Cognate with Hunsrik Pasdet.

parole.significato: princess (female member of a royal family other than a queen, especially a daughter or granddaughter)
parole.testo: From Prinzess(e) (“princess”) + -in (redundant female suffix). The former through Middle Dutch princesse from Old French princesse.

parole.significato: defined area of land, principally used for hunting or foraging
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German riviere (“undeveloped area; hunting ground; river”), borrowed, probably through Middle Dutch riviere (“river; riverside used for hunting birds”), from Old French riviere (“idem”), from Latin riparia (“riverside”). Cognate with modern Dutch rivier, English river, mod

From Middle High German scharlach, backformation from northern Middle High German scharlachen, from Middle Dutch scarlaken, alteration (based on Middle Dutch laken = German Laken) of older *scarlaten (early modern Dutch schaerlaten, southern Middle High German scharlāt), from Old French escarlate, f
From Middle High German tanz, from Middle Dutch dans, from Old French danse, dancier, equivalent to a deverbal from tanzen. See tanzen for more.

From Middle Dutch terpentijn, from Old French terbentine, turbentine, Latin terebinthīna, from terebintha, from Ancient Greek τερεβινθίνη (terebinthínē), from τερεβινθινος (terebinthinos), from τερέβινθος (terébinthos). See also turpentine.
